doc.title: Keith Ingham interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997

title: Arranging for singers and the cabaret scene versus modern music
summary: Ingham began arranging for singers, likes the cabaret scene, dislikes modern musical theater, and blames amateurs controlling the music business.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: When were you first able to use your arranging skills?

Well I’d done some things mostly with doing things for singers, you know Maxine Sullivan and just arranging stuff behind her. Because with singers it’s nice to have a little organized backing like we did tonight, we did those things behind Rebecca [Kilgore], it’s lovely. You know it makes all the difference because it gives it a nice little showcase setting for a singer. And I do like singers. A lot of musicians don’t like singers, but I like

it because you’re hearing the lyrics, and it’s good to work, I think there’s a very healthy cabaret scene. That’s one thing — I mean the jazz scene to me is not particularly, say interesting, it’s not, it doesn’t interest me much today, I mean what’s going on in contemporary ways, which may sound a bit fuddy duddy to you, but I don’t believe that anything that’s thirty, forty years old is particularly old. Perhaps we Europeans, we have a different time concept. But you know to me Jerome Kern and these melodies are as fresh as when they were first written, and you can still play them with absolute joy. But there is I think a cabaret scene, particularly in New York, where there are a lot of these young people who love this music. They either love the theater aspect of it or they like the cabaret singers, and they’re coming up, they’re digging into this great archive of American music. And there’s so much stuff out there, I mean it’s wonderful. I just recently saw on T.V. they did a tribute to Ira Gershwin, the lyricist. And he had found a song he wrote with Harry Warren, “There Is No Music For Me” or I think the title was “There Is No Music For Me.” I’d never heard that song. It was unpublished, and it’s a beauty, it’s an absolute gem. And there’s a show in London where they revived it, and that’s kind of contemporary. Of course it doesn’t get the attention that Andrew Lloyd Webber’s blown up nonsense gets you know, because that’s the blockbuster stuff, right? That’s Broadway now. But it’s there. There’s a show, funny enough, ironically, what’s the most successful show in London right now? It’s a show about Al Jolson. Yeah. Jolson of all things. Hopefully people will get sick of these elephantine productions of tuneless tunes. And oh God, I mean the stuff now, like “Jeckyl and Hyde” and stuff you have there, it’s just, I can’t describe it, it’s kind of melody in a way, but you can’t really say that this is a song, this isn’t a tune, it doesn’t have a beginning or end, it just sort of rambles on and rambles in the same basic kind of harmonies that can be understood in Saigon Uzbekistan, simple minded kind of melodies that are picked up anywhere in the world.
Yeah. Unfortunately it seems like the composers have delved into the harmonic schemes of Pop and Rock ‘n Roll—
Which certainly is not too rich compared to—

No. They’re not rich at all. I mean somebody said to me — I often wondered, I said, where did the change set in? He said, “when the amateurs took over the music business, the business side of it.” And I think that’s probably true. I think it probably came in with rock, whatever you want to say, but it was suddenly the people who began to control the tastes of what’s going to make a record and that, were not necessarily professional musicians.
